readings.c1s3:
''mold''<sup>3</sup>.] To change the form of; reduce from any form.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unmoulding'' reason’s mintage,
Charactered in the face.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 529.}}}}

'''unmolested''' (un-mọ̄-les′ted), ''a.'' Not molested; not disturbed; free from disturbance.
{{smaller block|<poem>Meanwhile the swains
Shall ''unmolested'' reap what plenty sows.</poem>
{{right|''J. Philips'', Cider, ii.}}}}

'''unmomentary''' (un-mō′men-tā-ri), ''a.'' At the same time, or without a moment’s intervention. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>From heav’n to earth He can descend, and bee
Aboue and here in space ''vnmomentarie.''</poem>
{{right|''Heywood'', Hierarchy of Angels, p. 439.}}}}

'''unmoneyed''' (un-mun′id), ''a.'' Not having money; not possessed of wealth: as, the ''unmoneyed'' classes. Also ''unmonied.''
{{smaller block|The ''unmoneyed'' wight. ''Shenstone'', The School-mistress.}}

'''unmonopolize''' (un-mọ̄-nop′ọ̄-līz), ''v. t.'' To free from monopoly; deprive of the character of a monopoly. Also ''unmonopolise.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The unappropriating and ''unmonopolizing'' the rewards of learning and industry from the greasie clutch of ignorance and high feeding.
{{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}}

'''unmonopolizing''' (un-mọ̄-nop′ọ̄-lī-zing), ''a.'' Not monopolizing; not including in a monopoly; not obtaining the whole of anything. Also ''unmonopolising.'' [Rare.]
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|The Duke hath all his goods moueable and ''unmoueable.''
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 242.}}}}

¶
'''unmovably†''' (un-mö′va̤-bli), ''adv.'' Immovably. Also ''unmoveably. Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), Pref., I. 16.

'''unmoved''' (un-mövd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not moved; not transferred from one place to another. ''Locke.'' —'''2.''' Not changed in purpose or resolution; unshaken; firm.
{{smaller block|''Unmoved'', unshaken, unseduced. ''Milton'', P. L., i. 554.}}
'''3.''' Not affected; not having the passions or feelings excited; not touched or impressed; not altered by passion or emotion; calm; apathetic: as, an ''unmoved'' heart; an ''unmoved'' look.
{{smaller block|<poem>Who, moving others, are themselves as stone,
''Unmoved'', cold, and to temptation slow.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, xciv.}}
<poem>Can you stand ''unmov’d''
When an earthquake of rebellion shakes the city,
And the court trembles?</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', False One, v. 4.}}
<poem>Who could dwell
''Unmoved'' upon the fate of one so young.</poem>
{{right|''Southey'', The Tale of Paraguay.}}}}

'''unmovedly†''' (un-mö′ved-li), ''adv.'' In an unmoved manner; without being moved.
{{smaller block|If you entreat, I will ''unmovedly'' hear.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, i. 2.}}}}

'''unmoving''' (un-mö′ving), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having no motion.
{{smaller block|''Unmoving'' heaps of matter. ''Cheyne'', Philos. Principles.
<poem>Alone, in thy cold skies,
Thou keep’st thy old ''unmoving'' station yet.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Hymn to the North Star.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''2.''' Not exciting emotion; having no power to affect the passions; unaffecting; not touching or impressive.

'''unmowed, unmown''' (un-mōd′, un-mōn′), ''a.'' Not mowed or cut down. ''Tennyson'', Arabian Nights.

'''unmuddle''' (un-mud′l), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''muddle.''] To free from muddle. See the quotation under ''unmeddle.'' [Rare.]

'''unmuffle''' (un-muf′l), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''muffle.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To take a muffler from, as the face; remove a muffler or wrapping from, as a person.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To throw off coverings or concealments.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unmuffle'', ye faint stars, and thou fair moon,
That wont’st to love the traveller’s benison.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 331.}}}}

'''unmultiply''' (un-mul′ti-plī), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''multiply.''] To reverse the process of multiplication in; separate into factors. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|As two factors multiplied together formed a product, it ought to be possible to ''unmultiply'' or split up (as “C. W. M.” expresses it) that product into its factors again.
{{right|''Nature'', XXXIX. 413.}}}}

'''unmunitioned''' (un-mū-nish′ọnd), ''a.'' Unfurnished with munitions of war.
{{smaller block|Cadiz, I told them, was held poor, unmanned, and ''unmunitioned.''
{{right|''Peeke'', Three to One, 1625 (Eng. Garner, i. 634). (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unmurmured''' (un-mėr′mėrd), ''a.'' Not murmured at. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>If my anger chance let fall a stroke,</poem>}}
readings.c3s3:
<poem>{{smaller block|As we are all subject to impetuous passions,
Yet it may pass ''unmurmur’d'', undisputed.
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''?), Nice Valour, iv. 1.}}}}</poem>

¶
'''unmurmuring''' (un-mėr′mėr-ing), ''a.'' Not murmuring; not complaining: as, ''unmurmuring'' patience. ''Byron'', Bride of Abydos, i. 13.

'''unmurmuringly''' (un-mėr′mėr-ing-li), ''adv.'' In an unmurmuring manner; uncomplainingly.

'''unmuscled''' (un-mus′ld), ''a.'' Having the muscles relaxed; flaccid: as, ''unmuscled'' cheeks. ''Richardson'', Clarissa Harlowe, VI. 362. (''Davies.'')

'''unmuscular''' (un-mus′kū-lär), ''a.'' Not muscular; physically weak. ''C. Reade'', Cloister and Hearth, lii. (''Davies.'')

'''unmusical''' (un-mū′zi-kal), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not musical; not harmonious or melodious; not pleasing to the ear.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let argument bear no ''unmusical'' sound,
Nor jars interpose, secret friendship to grieve.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Tavern Academy.}}
Milton could not have intended to close, not only a period, but a paragraph also, with an ''unmusical'' verse.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 296.}}}}
'''2.''' Not skilled in or fond of music: as, ''unmusical'' people.

'''unmusicality''' (un-mū-zi-kal′i̤-ti), ''n.'' The quality of being unmusical.
{{smaller block|The idea of ''unmusicality'' is a relative one.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXXVII. 356.}}}}

'''unmusically''' (un-mū′zi-kal-i), ''adv.'' In an unmusical manner; inharmoniously.
{{smaller block|[Landor’s] voice was sweet, and he could not speak ''unmusically'', though in a rage. ''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 65.}}

{{RunningHeader|unmitigable|6630|unmusically}}{{nop}}'''unmitigable''' (un-mit′i-ga-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being mitigated, softened, or lessened. {{smaller block|Her most ''unmitigable'' rage. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 276.}}}} '''unmitigated''' (un-mit′i-gā-ted), ''a.'' Not mitigated; not lessened; not softened or toned down; unassuaged; often, especially in colloquial use, unconscionable: as, an ''unmitigated'' scoundrel; an ''unmitigated'' lie. {{smaller block|With public accusation, uncovered slander, ''unmitigated'' rancour. {{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iv. 1. 308.}} The ''unmitigated'' blaze of vindicatory law. {{right|''J. W. Alexander'', Discourses, p. 62.}}}} '''unmitigatedly''' (un-mit′i-gā-ted-li), ''adv.'' Without mitigation; in an unmitigated degree; utterly. {{smaller block|“Lady Delmar” is neither realistic nor idealistic; it is altogether improbable and ''unmitigatedly'' melodramatic. {{right|''The Academy'', April 11, 1891, p. 342.}}}} '''unmixed, unmixt''' (un-mikst′), ''a.'' Not mixed; not mingled; pure; simple; unadulterated; unmingled; unalloyed. Thy commandment all alone shall live, . . . ''Unmix’d'' with baser matter. {{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 5. 104.}} God is an ''unmixed'' good. {{right|''T. Brooks'', Works, I. 187.}}}} '''unmixedly''' (un-mik′sed-li), ''adv.'' Entirely; purely; without mixture of other qualities; utterly. [Rare.] {{smaller block|That superstition cannot be regarded as ''unmixedly'' noxious which compels the hereditary master to kneel before the spiritual tribunal of the hereditary bondman. {{right|''Macaulay.''}}}} '''unmoaned''' (un-mōnd′), ''a.'' Not bemoaned or lamented. lamented. {{smaller block|Our fatherless distress was left ''unmoan’d.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 2. 64.}}}} '''unmodernize''' (un-mod′ėr-nīz), ''v. t.'' To alter from a modern fashion or style; give an ancient or old-fashioned form or fashion to. {{smaller block|''Unmodernize'' a poem rather than give it an antique air. {{right|''Lamb'', Essays.}}}} '''unmodifiable''' (un-mod′i-fī-a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not modifiable; not capable of being modified. '''unmodifiableness''' (un-mod′i-fī-a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being unmodifiable. {{smaller block|A nature not of brutish ''unmodifiableness.'' {{right|''George Eliot'', Daniel Deronda, lviii. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''unmodified''' (un-mod′i-fīd), ''a.'' Not modified; not altered in form; not qualified in meaning; not limited or circumscribed. {{smaller block|An universal, ''unmodified'' capacity to which the fanatics pretend. {{right|''Burke'', To Sir H. Langrishe.}}}} '''unmodish''' (un-mō′dish), ''a.'' Not modish; not according to custom or fashion; unfashionable; not stylish. {{smaller block|Your Eloquence would be needless—’tis so ''unmodish'' to need Persuasion. {{right|''Steele'', Tender Husband, v. 1.}}}} Who there frequents at these ''unmodish'' hours, But ancient matrons with their frizzled towers, And gray religious maids? {{smaller block|{{right|''Gay'', Eclogues, The Toilette.}}}} '''unmoistened''' (un-moi′snd), ''a.'' Not made moist or humid; not wetted; dry. And mayst thou die with an ''unmoisten’d'' eye, And no tear follow thee! {{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher (and another?)'', Nice Valour, ii. 1.}}}} '''unmold, unmould''' (un-mōld′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''mold''3.] To change the form of; reduce from any form. {{smaller block|''Unmoulding'' reason’s mintage, Charactered in the face. {{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 529.}}}} '''unmolested''' (un-mọ̄-les′ted), ''a.'' Not molested; not disturbed; free from disturbance. {{smaller block|Meanwhile the swains Shall ''unmolested'' reap what plenty sows. {{right|''J. Philips'', Cider, ii.}}}} '''unmomentary''' (un-mō′men-tā-ri), ''a.'' At the same time, or without a moment’s intervention. [Rare.] {{smaller block|From heav’n to earth He can descend, and bee Aboue and here in space ''vnmomentarie.'' {{right|''Heywood'', Hierarchy of Angels, p. 439.}}}} '''unmoneyed''' (un-mun′id), ''a.'' Not having money; not possessed of wealth: as, the ''unmoneyed'' classes. Also ''unmonied.'' {{smaller block|The ''unmoneyed'' wight. ''Shenstone'', The School-mistress.}} '''unmonopolize''' (un-mọ̄-nop′ọ̄-līz), ''v. t.'' To free from monopoly; deprive of the character of a monopoly. Also ''unmonopolise.'' [Rare.] {{smaller block|The unappropriating and ''unmonopolizing'' the rewards of learning and industry from the greasie clutch of ignorance and high feeding. {{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}} '''unmonopolizing''' (un-mọ̄-nop′ọ̄-lī-zing), ''a.'' Not monopolizing; not including in a monopoly; not obtaining the whole of anything. Also ''unmonopolising.'' [Rare.] {{smaller block|This is an important point, as suggesting the disinterested and ''unmonopolising'' side of æsthetic pleasure. {{right|''J. Sully'', Encyc. Brit., I. 216.}}}} '''unmoor''' (un-mör′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''moor''2.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' ''Naut.'', to bring to the state of riding with a single anchor, after having been moored by two or more cables.—'''2.''' To loose from anchorage or from moorings, literally or figuratively. {{smaller block|Thy skiff ''unmoor'', And waft us from the silent shore. {{right|''Byron'', Giaour.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To loose from moorings; weigh anchor. {{smaller block|Look, where beneath the castle grey His fleet ''unmoor'' from Aros bay! {{right|''Scott'', Lord of the Isles, i. 12.}}}} '''unmoral''' (un-mor′al), ''a.'' Not moral; non-moral; not a subject of moral attributes; neither moral nor immoral. '''unmorality''' (un-mọ̄-ral′ị-ti), ''n.'' Absence of morality; unmoral character. {{smaller block|The picture is very highly, a trifle too highly, wrought: but what pathos for those who can see behind it! The need of counsel, the lack of previous education, the absolute ''unmorality''. {{right|''The Academy'', Feb. 8, 1890, p. 94.}}}} '''unmoralized''' (un-mor′al-īzd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Untutored by morality; not conformed to good morals. [Rare.] {{smaller block|A dissolute and ''unmoralized'' temper. {{right|''Norris.''}}}} '''2.''' Not subjected to moralizing consideration: as, an ''unmoralized'' thought. {{smaller block|There are no cabinets of ''unmoralised'' or half-moralised conceptions, serving as illustrations of the evolution hypothesis. {{right|''New Princeton Rev.'', I. 180.}}}} Also ''unmoralised.'' '''unmoralizing''' (un-mor′al-ī-zing), ''a.'' '''1.''' Demoralizing.—'''2.''' Not given to or consisting in moral reflections. {{smaller block|He was primarily the artist, impersonal, ''unmoralizing,'' an eye and a vocabulary. {{right|''The Atlantic,'' LXIV. 701.}}}} '''unmorrised''' (un-mor′ist), ''a.'' [< ''un-''1 + ''morris'' + ''-ed''2.] Not dressed as a morris-dancer; not disguised by such a dress. [Rare.] What ails this fellow, Thus to appear before me ''unmorrised?'' {{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher,'' Women Pleased, iv. 1.}}}} '''unmortise''' (un-môr′tis), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''2 + ''mortise.''] To loosen or undo as a mortise; loosen the mortises or joints of. {{smaller block|In a dark nook stood an old broken-bottomed cane-couch, without a squab or cover-lid, sunk at one corner, and ''unmortised'' by the failing of one of its worm-eaten legs. {{right|''Richardson,'' Clarissa Harlowe, VI. 304.}}}} The wrist is parted from the hand that waved, The feet ''unmortised'' from their ankle-bones. {{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson,'' Merlin and Vivien.}}}} '''un-Mosaic''' (un-mọ̄-zā′ik), ''a.'' The reverse of Mosaic; contrary to Moses or his law. {{smaller block|By this reckoning Moses should be most ''un-Mosaic.'' {{right|''Milton.''}}}} '''unmothered''' (un-muᴛ̵ʜ′ėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not having a mother; deprived of a mother. [Rare.]—'''2†.''' Not having the feelings of a mother. I e’en quake to proceede. My spirit turnes edge. I feare me she’s ''unmother’d,'' yet I’ll venture. {{smaller block|{{right|''C. Tourneur,'' Revenger’s Tragedy, ii. 1.}}}} '''unmotherly''' (un-muᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-li), ''a.'' Not resembling or not befitting a mother. {{smaller block|''Unmotherly'' mother and unwomanly
Woman, that near turns motherhood to shame,
Womanliness to loathing. {{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 195.}}}} '''unmould''', ''v. t.'' See ''unmold.'' '''unmounted''' (un-moun′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not mounted; not performing regular duties on horseback: as, ''unmounted'' police.—'''2.''' Not furnished or set with appropriate or necessary appurtenances: as, an ''unmounted'' jewel; not affixed to a mount or backing, as of stiff paper or cardboard, as a drawing or a photograph; not provided with a mat of appropriate size and covered with a protecting glass, as a lantern-slide or transparency. '''unmourned''' (un-mōrnd′), ''a.'' Not mourned; not grieved for or lamented. {{smaller block|But still he goes ''unmourn’d'', returns unsought,
